title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two kinds of plot
Exploratory. You know what’s in it before you look. You make it, glance at it, move on. You’ll make hundreds and discard most.
Expository. Someone else has to read it — someone without your background and without much patience.
Getting from the first to the second takes real effort. This chapter is the toolkit.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)     # label and break helpers
library(ggrepel)    # non-overlapping text labels
library(patchwork)  # combining plots

Pair this chapter with a book about what to show, not just how. Cairo’s The Truthful Art is a good companion.






Note


label_info and potential_outliers (used later in this deck) are pre-computed in every live-code cell below, alongside mpg and diamonds.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
labs()

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway fuel economy (mpg)",
    color = "Car type",
    title = "Fuel efficiency generally decreases with engine size",
    subtitle = "Two seaters are an exception because of their light weight",
    caption = "Data from fueleconomy.gov"
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What each label is for



Label
Job




title
State the finding, not the plot’s contents


subtitle
Add detail, in smaller type below the title


caption
Usually the data source


x, y
Replace variable names with descriptions and units


aesthetic names
Same, for each legend









Tip


“A scatterplot of displacement vs. fuel economy” wastes the most prominent text on the slide describing what the reader can already see. Use the title to say what they should conclude.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mathematical labels
Swap the string for quote(); see ?plotmath for the vocabulary.

df <- tibble(x = 1:10, y = cumsum(x^2))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = quote(x[i]),
    y = quote(sum(x[i] ^ 2, i == 1, n))
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Build a plot from mpg with a custom title, subtitle, caption, x, y, and color.
Recreate a hwy vs. cty scatterplot where both color and shape vary by drive train.
Think of a graphic you’ve made recently — what title would state its finding rather than describe its axes?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Labels instead of a legend

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_info,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy, label = drive_type),
    fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = "right", vjust = "bottom"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


hjust and vjust control alignment relative to the anchor point.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
ggrepel fixes the overlap

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = label_info,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy, label = drive_type),
    fontface = "bold", size = 5, nudge_y = 2
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Highlighting specific points
A second layer of large hollow points draws the eye to the labelled cases:

potential_outliers <- mpg |> filter(hwy > 40 | (hwy > 20 & displ > 5))

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel(data = potential_outliers, aes(label = model)) +
  geom_point(data = potential_outliers, color = "red") +
  geom_point(
    data = potential_outliers,
    color = "red", size = 3, shape = "circle open"
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Other annotation geoms






Note



geom_hline() / geom_vline() — reference lines. Thick and white (linewidth = 2, color = "white"), drawn under the data, reads clearly without competing with it
geom_rect() — box off a region with xmin/xmax/ymin/ymax. ggforce’s geom_mark_hull() is a nicer alternative for irregular sets
geom_segment(arrow = ...) — point at something. x/y start, xend/yend end

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
annotate() for one-off text
Geoms highlight subsets of data; annotate() adds individual elements without needing a data frame.

trend_text <- "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy." |>
  str_wrap(width = 30)

trend_text

[1] "Larger engine sizes tend to\nhave lower fuel economy."


str_wrap() inserts line breaks at a chosen width.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Text plus arrow

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  annotate(
    geom = "label", x = 3.5, y = 38,
    label = trend_text, hjust = "left", color = "red"
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "segment",
    x = 3, y = 35, xend = 5, yend = 25, color = "red",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed")
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Use geom_text() with infinite positions to place text in all four corners.
Use annotate() to drop a single customized point in the middle of a plot.
How does geom_text() interact with faceting? How do you label just one facet? A different label in each?
Which geom_label() arguments control the background box?
What are the four arguments to arrow()?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Scales are always there
These two produce identical output:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class))

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  scale_x_continuous() +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  scale_color_discrete()

Naming scheme: scale_ + aesthetic + _ + scale type (continuous, discrete, date, datetime).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two reasons to override

Tweak the default — different breaks, different labels
Replace it entirely — a transformation or palette that fits your data better than a general-purpose default can

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Breaks and labels
Axes and legends are collectively called guides. breaks sets where the ticks or keys go; labels sets what they say.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(15, 40, by = 5))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Suppressing and renaming
labels = NULL removes them entirely — useful for maps, or when you can’t publish absolute numbers. For discrete scales, pass a named vector.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c("4" = "4-wheel", "f" = "front", "r" = "rear"))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Formatting with the scales package
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar())
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1/1000, suffix = "K"),
    breaks = seq(1000, 19000, by = 6000)
  )










Note breaks stays in the original data scale.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Percentages

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Percentage", labels = label_percent())

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Breaks that mark real events
With few data points, put the ticks where the observations are:

presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = start, y = id)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = end, yend = id)) +
  scale_x_date(name = NULL, breaks = presidential$start, date_labels = "'%y")


Dates use date_labels (a format string) and date_breaks ("2 days", "1 month").

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Legend position
legend.position is a theme setting:
base <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + geom_point(aes(color = class))

base + theme(legend.position = "right")
base + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))










Short and wide → top or bottom. Tall and narrow → left or right. "none" removes it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Overriding legend aesthetics

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 4)))








Warning


Legend keys inherit whatever aesthetics the layer uses — including a low alpha. Plot many points at alpha = 1/20 and the legend swatches become nearly invisible. override.aes = list(alpha = 1) (or size = ... as above) fixes the legend without touching the data layer.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Transform in the scale, not the mapping
text:
Transform in the scale, not the mapping
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = log10(carat), y = log10(price))) +
  geom_bin2d()
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()
















Note


Visually identical — but the right-hand axes are labelled in the original units. Transforming inside aes() leaves the reader staring at log values; transforming via the scale keeps the plot interpretable.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Color: ColorBrewer
The default categorical palette spaces hues evenly around the color wheel. ColorBrewer’s palettes are hand-tuned so common forms of color blindness can still distinguish them.
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + geom_point(aes(color = drv))
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Redundant encoding is simpler still






Tip


With only a few categories, map shape and color to the same variable. It survives color blindness, photocopying, and black-and-white printing — cheap insurance for very little extra code.




ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv, shape = drv)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
When the mapping is predetermined
Some variables come with expected colors. scale_color_manual() pins them down:

presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = start, y = id, color = party)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = end, yend = id)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Republican = "#E81B23", Democratic = "#00AEF3"))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Continuous color: viridis
Designed to be perceptually uniform and legible in grayscale. Available as continuous (_c), discrete (_d), and binned (_b).
df <- tibble(x = rnorm(10000), y = rnorm(10000))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_hex() + coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Default", x = NULL, y = NULL)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_hex() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Viridis", x = NULL, y = NULL)










Every color scale exists as both scale_color_*() and scale_fill_*(), in US and UK spellings.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Three ways to set limits

Filter the data
Set limits on the scale
Set xlim/ylim in coord_cartesian()







Caution


Options 1 and 2 both throw data away before any stat or smooth is fit — a geom_smooth() curve will genuinely change shape. Option 3 is a true zoom: the smooth is fit on the full data and only the view changes. Pick option 3 unless you actually want to refit on a subset.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zooming, demonstrated
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) + geom_smooth() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 25))
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) + geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 6), ylim = c(10, 25))










Same window, different smooth curves — the left one refit on a subset.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Expanding limits to share scales
limits is genuinely useful in the other direction: making separate plots comparable.
suv     <- mpg |> filter(class == "suv")
compact <- mpg |> filter(class == "compact")

x_scale   <- scale_x_continuous(limits = range(mpg$displ))
y_scale   <- scale_y_continuous(limits = range(mpg$hwy))
col_scale <- scale_color_discrete(limits = unique(mpg$drv))

ggplot(suv, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() + x_scale + y_scale + col_scale
ggplot(compact, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() + x_scale + y_scale + col_scale

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Why doesn’t scale_color_gradient() change anything on a geom_hex() plot?
What’s the first argument to every scale? How does it relate to labs()?
Improve the presidential terms plot: combine the color and break customizations, fix the y axis, label each term with a name, add proper labels, and place breaks every four years.
Use override.aes to make a legend readable when alpha = 1/20.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Built-in themes

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw()


Eight ship with ggplot2: theme_gray() (default), theme_bw(), theme_light(), theme_classic(), theme_linedraw(), theme_dark(), theme_minimal(), theme_void(). ggthemes adds many more.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Why is the default background gray?
text:
Why is the default background gray?






Note


Deliberate. The white grid lines stay visible — they matter for position judgments — without shouting. The gray gives the panel a typographic weight similar to surrounding text, so plots sit in a document instead of leaping off the page. And the continuous field of color makes the plot read as one object.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Customizing individual components
theme() controls everything non-data. element_*() functions describe how each piece looks.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.6, 0.7),
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Worth knowing

element_text() — font face, size, color, justification
element_rect() — backgrounds and borders
element_line() — grid lines and axis lines
element_blank() — remove a component entirely

plot.title.position = "plot" aligns the title to the whole graphic rather than the panel, which usually looks better with left-aligned captions.
See ?theme for the full list.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
patchwork
Save plots as objects, then combine them with operators:

p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() + labs(title = "Plot 1")
p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "Plot 2")

p1 + p2


patchwork doesn’t add a new function here — it teaches + a new trick.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Composing layouts
| places side by side, / starts a new row.

p3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() + labs(title = "Plot 3")

(p1 | p3) / p2

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Collecting legends

p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, cty, color = drv)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = "Plot 1")
p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = "Plot 2")
p3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, color = drv, fill = drv)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + labs(title = "Plot 3")
p4 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy, color = drv, fill = drv)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + labs(title = "Plot 4")
p5 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) + facet_wrap(~drv) + labs(title = "Plot 5")

(guide_area() / (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4) / p5) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "City and highway mileage for cars with different drive trains",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(1, 3, 2, 4)) &
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What just happened

guide_area() reserves a slot for the shared legend
plot_layout(guides = "collect") gathers legends from every panel into it
heights = c(1, 3, 2, 4) divides the vertical space proportionally







Note


& applies a theme setting to every plot in the patchwork; a plain + would only affect the last one added. This is the one place in ggplot2 code where & and + are not interchangeable — worth flagging explicitly.



More at https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What changes if you drop the parentheses from (p1 | p2) / p3? Why?
Build a patchwork where Plot 1 spans the top row and Plots 2 and 3 share the second row, tagged “Fig. A”, “Fig. B”, “Fig. C”.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

Labels — the title states the finding; axes carry units
Annotations — geom_text()/ggrepel for data, annotate() for one-offs; reference lines, rectangles, and arrows all help
Scales — breaks and labels to tweak, whole scales to replace; transform in the scale so axes stay readable
Color — ColorBrewer and viridis for accessibility; redundant shape encoding is free insurance
Zooming — coord_cartesian() zooms, limits subsets
Themes — everything that isn’t data
Layout — patchwork for multi-panel figures

text:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Where we are
Chapter 1 gave you a working template for plots. This chapter explains why that template works.
By the end you should be able to describe any ggplot2 plot in terms of seven components:

data
aesthetic mappings
a geom
a stat
a position adjustment
a coordinate system
a faceting scheme


Frame this as moving from “recipes” to “grammar”. Once students see the seven slots, unfamiliar plots stop looking like new syntax to memorize.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)

We’ll work mostly with two datasets that ship with ggplot2:

mpg — 234 car models, 11 variables
diamonds — ~54,000 diamonds


mpg |> select(manufacturer, model, displ, hwy, class, drv) |> head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  manufacturer model displ   hwy class   drv  
  <chr>        <chr> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <chr>
1 audi         a4      1.8    29 compact f    
2 audi         a4      1.8    29 compact f    
3 audi         a4      2      31 compact f    
4 audi         a4      2      30 compact f    








Note


Every dataset in this deck (mpg, diamonds, smaller, label_info, …) is already loaded in the live-code cells below via a hidden setup chunk — you don’t need to re-run library(tidyverse) yourself before trying an exercise.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Mapping a variable to an aesthetic
text:
Mapping a variable to an aesthetic
An aesthetic is a visual property of the marks on the plot: position, color, shape, size, transparency.
aes() says “let this variable control that property.”

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Not every aesthetic suits every variable
text:
Not every aesthetic suits every variable
shape only supplies six distinct symbols before it gives up — a seventh category simply goes unplotted, with a warning.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = class)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: The shape palette can deal with a maximum of 6 discrete values because more
than 6 becomes difficult to discriminate
ℹ you have requested 7 values. Consider specifying shapes manually if you need
  that many of them.


Warning: Removed 62 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Warning


class has seven levels but shape can only display six. SUVs (62 rows) silently disappear from the plot above — always read the warnings ggplot2 gives you, they’re telling you data went missing from the picture.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Ordered aesthetics imply ordered data
size and alpha are ranked channels. Mapping an unordered category to them tells the reader a ranking exists when it doesn’t.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = class)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Using size for a discrete variable is not advised.









Caution


class (2seater, compact, midsize, …) has no inherent order. Mapping it to size or alpha visually implies “bigger/darker = more,” which is misleading for a purely categorical variable. Save these aesthetics for variables that are genuinely ordered or continuous.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mapping vs. setting
Inside aes() = mapping, driven by data, gets a legend. Outside aes() = setting, a fixed constant, no legend.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2, shape = 17)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setting values
When you set an aesthetic you supply a raw value, not a variable:



Aesthetic
Value




color
a color name or hex string, "blue", "#E81B23"


size
point size in mm, size = 1


shape
an integer 0–25, shape = 1


alpha
opacity from 0 to 1



Shapes 0–14 are hollow (border from color), 15–20 are solid (filled with color), and 21–25 take both a color border and a fill.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Draw hwy vs. displ with pink filled triangles.
Why does the code below not produce blue points?
What does stroke do, and which shapes respond to it? (?geom_point)
What happens with aes(color = displ < 5)?





ggplot(mpg) +
  geom_point(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = "blue"))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: A geom is how the data gets drawn
text:
A geom is how the data gets drawn
Same data, same mappings, different geom:



ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point()










ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_smooth()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Geoms accept different aesthetics
A line has no shape; a point has no linetype. ggplot2 quietly ignores aesthetics a geom can’t use.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, linetype = drv)) +
  geom_smooth()


Mapping a discrete variable splits the geom into one object per level.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Grouping without a legend
group splits the data the same way, but adds no legend and no visual distinction.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = drv))








Note


group is what mapping a discrete variable does implicitly behind the scenes — using it explicitly is handy when you want the splitting behaviour without the legend or the visual distinction that color or linetype would add.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Layers stack
Multiple geoms in one plot. Mappings in ggplot() are global; mappings in a geom are local to that layer.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Layers can have their own data
text:
Layers can have their own data
Useful for highlighting a subset:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(
    data = mpg |> filter(class == "2seater"),
    color = "red", size = 2
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Different geoms reveal different things
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_density()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()













The histogram and density show bimodality and right skew; the boxplot compresses that into a summary but flags outliers.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Beyond the built-in geoms
ggplot2 ships with 40+ geoms.






Tip


If you need a geom that doesn’t exist, check the extension gallery before writing your own: https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/. Someone has often already solved the problem — e.g. ggridges for ridgeline plots.




library(ggridges)

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = drv, fill = drv, color = drv)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Which geom draws a line chart? A boxplot? A histogram? An area chart?
What does show.legend = FALSE do, and why might you want it?
What does se control in geom_smooth()?
Recreate a plot with points colored by drv and one smooth curve fitted to the whole dataset (not one per group).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
facet_wrap(): one variable
Splits the plot into panels, one per level.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
facet_grid(): two variables
A two-sided formula, rows ~ cols.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(drv ~ cyl)


Empty panels mean that combination doesn’t occur in the data.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Free scales
By default every panel shares one scale, which is what makes panels comparable. Release that with scales:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(drv ~ cyl, scales = "free")








Note


"free_x", "free_y", or "free" let each row/column pick its own range — easier to read within a panel, but panels are no longer directly comparable to each other. Use free scales for exploration, shared scales for communication.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What happens if you facet on a continuous variable?
What does . mean in facet_grid(drv ~ .)?
Faceting vs. the color aesthetic — when is each better? Does the answer change as the dataset grows?
Which reads better for comparing displ across drive trains: faceting by row or by column? What does that suggest as a rule of thumb?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Where does count come from?

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut)) +
  geom_bar()


count isn’t a column in diamonds. The bar geom computed it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stats
A stat is the algorithm a geom runs on your data before drawing.

bar charts, histograms, freqpolys → bin and count
smoothers → fit a model, plot predictions
boxplots → compute a five-number summary

Every geom has a default stat; every stat has a default geom. ?geom_bar tells you it uses stat_count(), and lists the variables it computes.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Using a computed variable
after_stat() reaches into the variables the stat produced.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) +
  geom_bar()








Important


Without group = 1, each bar is treated as its own group and every proportion comes out as 1 — there’s nothing to divide by. Try deleting group = 1 in the live cell below and see what happens.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Calling a stat directly
Sometimes the summary is the point, and naming the stat says so:

ggplot(diamonds) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    fun.min = min, fun.max = max, fun = median
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What geom does stat_summary() use by default? Rewrite the previous plot with it.
How does geom_col() differ from geom_bar()?
List some geom/stat pairs. What do they have in common?
Why did the proportion bar chart need group = 1? Confirm by removing it in the cell below.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
color vs. fill for bars
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, color = drv)) + geom_bar()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = drv)) + geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stacking is a position adjustment
Map fill to a second variable and the bars stack automatically:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = class)) +
  geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The four options
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = class)) + geom_bar(position = "fill")
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = class)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge")











"stack" — the default for bars
"fill" — stack, then normalize each bar to the same height: compares proportions
"dodge" — side by side: compares individual counts
"identity" — draw where the values fall; overlaps for bars, default for points

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Overplotting
hwy and displ are rounded, so points land on a grid and pile up. This scatterplot shows 126 visible points for 234 observations.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Jittering
position = "jitter" adds a little random noise. Less accurate at small scales, far more honest at large ones.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_jitter()


geom_jitter() is shorthand for geom_point(position = "jitter").

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What’s wrong with a plain geom_point() of cty vs. hwy? Fix it below.
Is there any difference between the default and position = "identity" for points? Why?
Which arguments to geom_jitter() control the amount of jitter?
Compare geom_jitter() and geom_count().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The default is Cartesian
x and y act independently. Two alternatives come up often enough to know:

coord_quickmap() — fixes the aspect ratio for geographic data
coord_polar() — bends the Cartesian plane into polar coordinates


nz <- map_data("nz")

ggplot(nz, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "white", color = "black") +
  coord_quickmap()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Polar coordinates
A bar chart and a Coxcomb chart are the same plot in different coordinates:
bar <- ggplot(diamonds) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = clarity, fill = clarity), show.legend = FALSE, width = 1) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

bar + coord_flip()
bar + coord_polar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Why this matters
Any plot you can imagine is some combination of:
data → stat → geom → aesthetic mappings → coordinate system → position → facets
Change one slot, get a different plot. That’s the whole idea behind “the layered grammar of graphics,” and it’s why you can build hundreds of thousands of plots from one template.
The original paper is worth reading: https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/layered-grammar.pdf

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

Aesthetics map variables to visual properties; setting differs from mapping
Geoms decide how marks are drawn; layers stack and can override data and mappings
Facets split one plot into comparable panels
Stats compute the values a geom actually plots
Positions resolve overlap: stack, fill, dodge, jitter
Coordinates redefine what x and y mean

Still to come: themes, in Chapter 11.

Package reference — https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference

ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis — https://ggplot2-book.org/

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Choosing How to Show Data







Quick distinctions



Continuous: a numeric value that can (in theory) take any value in a range.
Categorical: falls into one of several unordered groups (nominal) or has only two options (binary).
Likert: an ordered scale (e.g., “very difficult” → “difficult” → … → “very manageable”)

categorical, but with a meaningful order.













One idea to hold onto


The type of variable decides the type of plot.

One category at a time → bar chart
One number at a time → histogram
Two things at once → scatterplot (or boxplot, if one is a category)

Initializing R packages

Use install.packages("package_name") in the console to install R packages on your own machine.

Example: install.packages("ggplot2") to install ggplot2.

Use library(package_name) to initialize already installed packages.

Example: library(ggplot2) to load ggplot2.

To install the package if it isn’t already installed and then initialize it after installation:

if(!require(package_name)) install.packages("package_name")
library(package_name)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Assigning Variables

The operators =, <-, and -> can be used to assign values to variables

If we want to assign x = 2; x=2, x<-2, and 2->x are equivalent.
Common convention is to use <- but feel free to use =.

Rules for variable names.

Start with a letter (x5 is OK but 5x is NOT.)
Consist of letters, numbers, underscores, and periods (x_5 and x.5 are OK but not x-5).
Case sensitive (x and X would be different variables).

Variable naming conventions

Try to use meaningful names.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Displaying Output

R will display the outputs of unassigned calculations

exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) (approximately) and display the result.

R suppresses the output of assigned calculations

x<-exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) and store the result in x but would not display anything.
To see that value of x we would need to run print(x) or just x.

Workspace (Environment)

Use ls() or objects() to generate a list of objects. in workspace.
Use rm() to remove objects from the current workspace.

The call rm(x,y,z) will remove the variables x, y, and z from the workspace.
The call rm(list=ls()) will remove all objects from the workspace.
The workspace is automatically cleared when RStudio is exited.

text:
Before we look at the raw data…







Thinking Moment


What do you think could go wrong with real, raw survey data?











Potential Problems


What kinds of problems might it have that yesterday’s polished plots didn’t show?

Here’s the actual raw file

survey_2017_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2017.csv")

# Note the skip = 1 -- 2022's file has a stray metadata line above the

glimpse(survey_2017_raw)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Duplicate responses (rows)
A few respondents show up more than once. - Think of this as a double-submitted survey.

survey_2017_raw |> count(respondent_id, sort = TRUE) |> filter(n > 1)

survey_2017_raw <- survey_2017_raw |> distinct()
survey_2022_raw <- survey_2022_raw |> distinct()


The function distinct() removes exact duplicate rows. It is always worth checking for before doing anything else), since duplicates quietly inflate every count.

Strings & expressions







The format for income response is a mess!


Sometimes people are allowed to type in their responses however they like. For example, if someone has an annual income of $85,000, there are several ways they might enter that in the survey:

"85000"
"$85,000"
"85,000"
"85K"

So how do we take all these different formats and turn them into something we can actually work with in our analysis?

For Question 7 of the survey, I asked everyone what was the best sandwich?







Most Popular Answer

Grilled cheese
Grilled Cheese
Grilled Cheese!
grilled cheese
grilled cheese with Hot sauce

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: provinces
Same province, several spellings: "Ontario", "ON", "ontario ".

standardize_province <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("ontario", "on") ~ "Ontario",
    x %in% c("alberta", "ab") ~ "Alberta",
    x %in% c("british columbia", "bc") ~ "British Columbia",
    x %in% c("quebec", "qc") ~ "Quebec",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(x)
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: Yes/No
We might get three variations for the same two answers: "Yes"/"No", "Y"/"N", "yes"/"no".

standardize_yn <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("yes", "y") ~ "Yes",
    x %in% c("no", "n") ~ "No",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing data







Where did missing data come from?


Sometimes we don’t always get all the complete data set that we want.

People tend to skip questions that they don’t feel comfortable answer.
perhaps people forgot to fill in one of the questions/pages of survey.
maybe people gave some weird looking answer that is unusable (e.g $*@2#$1aE&)
or sometimes these questions are simply irrelevant to them

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 1) Delete the row
If a respondent didn’t answer a question in the survey, we can just remove this person entirely from the data analysis. :)







This is cool, but…


While this is a simple method, you will lose the respondents.

if the people who skipped the question aren’t random, the ones left behind don’t represent everyone fairly.






survey_2017_nomiss <- survey_2017_clean |>
  drop_na(income, savings_pct,
          debt_overwhelmed,
          emergency_fund_likelihood)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 2) Imputation
Instead of throwing the whole response away, we can guess a reasonable value to put in its place.

like using the average of everyone else’s answer. (e.g. mean or median)


survey_2017_clean |> mutate(income = ifelse(is.na(income), median(income, na.rm = TRUE), income))








This is cool, but…


Now some of your “data” is really just a guess. If you fill in too many values this way, your data can look more similar than it actually is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched response







Too many response levels


Sometimes survey designers choose a set of response options one year, then decide to change them the next. For example, in our financial wellness data, the survey asked questions of How difficult is it to obtain $2,000 of emergency fund?:

in 2017, there are 7 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Somewhat difficult, Neither, Somewhat manageable, Manageable, Very manageable
in 2022, there are now only 5 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Neither, Manageable, Very manageable

So what do you do? Neither of them directly match each other. And this is difficult for a year-to-year comparative analysis

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Potential Solution







Compromise


We can collapse both down to 3 levels — Difficult, Neither, Manageable.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult", "Somewhat difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Somewhat manageable", "Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Before: 7 Levels vs 5 Levels

Different number of categories, different wording. It is not easy to tell how people have changed over time by comparing these two bar plots side by side as-is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
After:

Now that both years use the same 3 levels, we can finally put them side by side and ask: did things get better, worse, or stay the same?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Different ways of asking the same question
text:
Different ways of asking the same question







Mismatched question: same question, different name


Sometimes a question gets worded differently across years, even though it’s really asking the same thing.

in 2017, the survey asked How difficult was it for you if your paycheque is delayed?

stored as paycheque_delay_difficulty

in 2022, the question became If there is a two week delay in your paycheque arrival, how impactful would it be to your finances?

stored as twoweek_pay_delay_impact


Same underlying question, different wording and different column name — rename() fixes this in one line each.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched responses: Age

survey_2017_clean |> select(age) |> head()
survey_2022_clean |> select(age) |> head()








Are you willing to share your age?


Sometimes the same underlying question gets measured differently across years, even when the intent is identical.

in 2017, respondents gave an exact age

stored as age, e.g. 34

in 2022, respondents picked from age brackets instead

stored as age, e.g. "30-40"

Now we have the same underlying question, but a different level of precision

In order to compare over the years, everyone needs to speak the same bucket language.







survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(age_bucket = case_when(
    age <= 30 ~ "18-30",
    age <= 40 ~ "30-40",
    age <= 50 ~ "40-50",
    age <= 65 ~ "50-65",
    TRUE ~ "65+"
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  rename(age_bucket = age)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Removed benefit option: aligning categories







Non-existent Option in Survey


“Educational funding” existed as a choice in 2017, but the 2022 platform dropped it. To compare years fairly, we fold anything not offered in both years into a shared “Other” category.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(benefit_preference = if_else(
    benefit_preference == "benefit_education",
    "benefit_other",
    benefit_preference
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Combine into one data set

survey_combined <- bind_rows(survey_2017_clean, survey_2022_clean)

glimpse(survey_combined)








Only possible now


Now that we have:
— column names match (rename()) - category sets match (the “Other” recoded) - response scales match (the 3-level of likert responses in paycheque question)
Every fix so far existed to make this one line possible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Too much info in one column
text:
Too much info in one column







One column doing two jobs


The variable respondent_id looks like a single value, but it’s actually smuggling in two separate pieces of information at once.

the year the response came from, e.g. 2017
the respondent’s number within that year, e.g. 0001

Both are jammed into one string: "2017-0001". If we ever want to work with just the year, or just the respondent number, we’re stuck first pulling them apart.





survey_combined <- survey_combined |>
  separate(respondent_id, into = c("survey_year", "respondent_num"), sep = "-")

survey_combined |>
  select(survey_year, respondent_num, everything()) |>
  head()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Show concluding results

survey_combined |>
  ggplot(aes(x = financial_wellness_cluster, y = income, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  labs(title = "Income by Cluster: 2017 vs 2022",
       x = "Cluster", y = "Income ($)", fill = "Year") +
  theme_minimal()


This is the exact plot style from Day 1, except now you’ve watched every step of how the data underneath it got here.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Back to your predictions







Discussion


Which of your guesses from the start of class came true?
What did we run into that nobody predicted?











Document your decisions


A results plot without its cleaning log is a claim without evidence. For any real report, this deserves its own short section (ahem your final report):

Which rows/columns were dropped, and why
Every recoding decision (e.g. collapsing levels and combining buckets, etc.)
What’s imputed vs. observed, clearly marked

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A few cautions







Keep in mind



Every cleaning choice was also an analytical choice — a different 3-level collapse, a different age-bucket rule, a different imputation method could all shift what we find downstream
This dataset is synthetic: today’s numbers are illustrative, not a claim about real Canadians
Later this semester: missing-data methods and statistical tests that let you make these calls more rigorously than by eyeballing












Next Week


We will actually begin learning how to code! Starting with Visualization.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The EDA loop
EDA is not a procedure with a checklist. It’s a cycle you run until the questions stop being interesting:

Generate questions about your data
Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modelling
Refine your questions, or generate new ones from what you found

Most of what you produce during EDA gets thrown away. That’s fine — the output is understanding, not plots.

Emphasize that dead ends are expected and not failure. Students often think EDA should look tidy in retrospect.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Why it’s not optional
Even when the research question arrives fully formed, you still have to know whether the data can answer it.
Data cleaning is a special case of EDA: you’re asking whether the data meets your expectations, and using the same tools — visualization, transformation, modelling — to find out.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)

Two guiding questions carry most of the weight:

What variation occurs within my variables?
What covariation occurs between my variables?







Note


smaller (diamonds filtered to carat < 3) is already available in every live cell below, along with mpg and diamonds.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation
Variation is the tendency of a variable’s values to change from one measurement to the next.
Measure anything continuous twice and you get two answers — even for quantities that are genuinely constant. Add real differences between subjects and across time, and every variable gets its own characteristic pattern.
The way to see that pattern is to plot the distribution.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A first look

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Binwidth changes what you can see
text:
Binwidth changes what you can see

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)


Same data. A much narrower bin reveals structure the first plot hid entirely.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Typical values: what to ask
Tall bars are common values, short bars rare ones, gaps are values never observed. Turn that into questions:

Which values are most common? Why?
Which are rare? Does that match what you expected?
Are there unexpected patterns? What could explain them?

For the carat histogram: why the spikes at whole carats and common fractions? And why more diamonds just above each spike than just below?

The answer involves both cutting practice and pricing incentives — a good illustration that some EDA questions need domain knowledge, not more code.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Clusters mean subgroups
When a distribution separates into clumps, ask:

How are observations within a cluster alike?
How do clusters differ from each other?
What explains the split?
Could the clusters be an artifact rather than real structure?

Many of these push you toward a relationship between variables.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Unusual values hide in plain sight
text:
Unusual values hide in plain sight

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)


The only hint of anything odd is how wide the x-axis is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zoom in on the y-axis

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))


Now three unusual regions show up: near 0, around 30, and around 60.






Note


coord_cartesian() zooms — the bars are still computed from all the data, so you can safely zoom the y-axis to see rare bins without changing what got counted. ylim()/xlim() instead discard any data outside the limits before the stat runs, which can silently change your bar heights. When you just want a closer look, reach for coord_cartesian().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Pull the outliers out

unusual <- diamonds |>
  filter(y < 3 | y > 20) |>
  select(price, x, y, z) |>
  arrange(y)

unusual

# A tibble: 9 × 4
  price     x     y     z
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  5139  0      0    0   
2  6381  0      0    0   
3 12800  0      0    0   
4 15686  0      0    0   
5 18034  0      0    0   
6  2130  0      0    0   
7  2130  0      0    0   
8  2075  5.15  31.8  5.12
9 12210  8.09  58.9  8.06

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What we found
y is a dimension in millimeters. A diamond cannot be 0 mm wide, so those rows are missing data encoded as zero — something no search for NA would ever have surfaced.
The 32 mm and 59 mm entries are implausible too: over an inch across, but priced like ordinary stones.






Important


This is the core payoff of EDA: visualizing the data surfaced a data-quality problem that a search for NA never would have. Always sanity-check units and physically-plausible ranges, not just missingness flags.









Caution


Run your analysis with and without the outliers. If it barely moves and you can’t explain them, dropping them is defensible. If it moves a lot, find the cause and disclose the removal in your write-up — don’t drop values without justification just because they’re inconvenient.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two ways to handle them

# Option 1: drop the whole row — usually too blunt
diamonds2 <- diamonds |> filter(between(y, 3, 20))

# Option 2: replace the bad value with NA — usually better
diamonds2 <- diamonds |>
  mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))

One invalid measurement doesn’t invalidate the rest of the observation. Apply option 1 across every variable in messy data and you may have nothing left.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values in plots
ggplot2 won’t guess where to put an NA, so it drops them and warns you. Silence the warning with na.rm = TRUE — once you’ve understood why they’re missing.

diamonds2 <- diamonds |> mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missingness can be the signal
In nycflights13::flights, a missing dep_time means the flight was cancelled. So compare scheduled departure times for cancelled and non-cancelled flights:

nycflights13::flights |>
  mutate(
    cancelled = is.na(dep_time),
    sched_hour = sched_dep_time %/% 100,
    sched_min  = sched_dep_time %% 100,
    sched_dep_time = sched_hour + (sched_min / 60)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sched_dep_time)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cancelled), binwidth = 1/4)








Tip


Missing values aren’t always noise to drop. Sometimes why a value is missing is itself the most informative variable in the dataset — is.na(dep_time) here is doing more analytical work than dep_time itself.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The comparison isn’t fair yet
Cancelled flights are vastly outnumbered, so the two curves aren’t comparable on a count scale.
That’s a covariation problem — and the next section is about fixing exactly this kind of comparison.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Explore the distributions of x, y, and z in diamonds. Which is length, which width, which depth?
Explore price. Try a wide range of binwidths. Anything surprising?
How many diamonds are 0.99 carat vs. exactly 1 carat? Why the gap?
Compare coord_cartesian() with xlim()/ylim() when zooming into a histogram.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Covariation
If variation describes behavior within a variable, covariation describes behavior between variables: the tendency for two or more variables to move together.
The strategy depends on the variable types:

categorical × numerical
categorical × categorical
numerical × numerical

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Categorical × numerical: the count problem

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)


Group sizes differ so much that shape differences are invisible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Switch the y-axis to density
Density is the count standardized so the area under each curve is 1. Since it isn’t a column in the data, after_stat() fetches it from the stat.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A surprise
Fair diamonds — the lowest quality cut — appear to have the highest average price.
Frequency polygons are busy, though. A boxplot makes the comparison cleaner:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Important


This is a genuine paradox, not a plotting artifact — worse-cut diamonds really do look more expensive here. Hold onto this; the “Patterns and models” section resolves it once carat enters the picture.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reordering unordered categories
cut is an ordered factor, so its order is meaningful. Most categorical variables aren’t.






Tip


fct_reorder(variable, by, fun) sorts factor levels by a summary statistic of another variable — almost always makes a categorical-vs-numeric plot easier to read at a glance.



ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Flip when labels are long
Swap the x and y mappings — no extra function needed:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median))) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Improve the cancelled-vs-non-cancelled departure time plot.
Which variable best predicts diamond price? How is it related to cut? Use that to explain why poorer cuts look more expensive.
Compare swapping x/y with adding coord_flip().
Try geom_violin(), a faceted geom_histogram(), a colored geom_freqpoly(), and a colored geom_density() on the same comparison. What does each do well and badly?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Categorical × categorical: counts

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = color)) +
  geom_count()


Circle area shows how many observations fall at each combination.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Or compute the counts, then tile
text:
Or compute the counts, then tile

diamonds |>
  count(color, cut) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = color, y = cut)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = n))








Note


For unordered categories, the seriation package can reorder rows and columns to expose structure; heatmaply does interactive versions of the same idea for larger tables.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Numerical × numerical

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point()


A positive, roughly exponential relationship — and a lot of overplotting.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Transparency helps

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1 / 100)


Clusters at 1, 1.5, and 2 carats become visible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Bin in two dimensions
ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) + geom_bin2d()
ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) + geom_hex()










geom_bin2d() uses rectangles, geom_hex() hexagons (needs the hexbin package). Both map bin counts to fill.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Or bin one variable and reuse boxplots
text:
Or bin one variable and reuse boxplots

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(group = cut_width(carat, 0.1)))


cut_width(x, width) slices x into equal-width bins. cut_number() makes bins with roughly equal counts instead.

Boxplots look about the same regardless of how many points they summarize. varwidth = TRUE makes box width proportional to group size, which is worth mentioning here.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Frequency polygon instead of boxplot for the conditional distribution — what changes? When does cut_width() beat cut_number()?
Visualize carat partitioned by price.
How do price distributions compare for very large vs. very small diamonds?
Combine two techniques to show cut, carat, and price together.
Why is a scatterplot better than a binned plot for spotting 2-D outliers?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Interrogating a pattern
A systematic relationship shows up as a pattern. When you spot one, ask:

Could this be coincidence?
How would you describe the relationship?
How strong is it?
What other variables might be involved?
Does it hold within subgroups?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation vs. covariation
Variation creates uncertainty. Covariation reduces it.
If two variables covary, values of one improve your predictions about the other. If the covariation is causal — a special case — you can use one to control the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Models extract patterns
The cut/price paradox exists because carat is entangled with both. Fit a model for price from carat, then look at what’s left over.

library(tidymodels)

diamonds <- diamonds |>
  mutate(log_price = log(price), log_carat = log(carat))

diamonds_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(log_price ~ log_carat, data = diamonds)

diamonds_aug <- augment(diamonds_fit, new_data = diamonds) |>
  mutate(.resid = exp(.resid))

Log-transform first, fit, then exponentiate the residuals back to a price-like scale.






Note


tidymodels is heavy and not part of the live-code package set for this deck, so this example stays static — run it locally in RStudio if you’d like to reproduce it yourself.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The paradox dissolves

ggplot(diamonds_aug, aes(x = cut, y = .resid)) +
  geom_boxplot()

With the carat effect removed, the expected relationship appears: relative to their size, better-cut diamonds cost more.
Modelling gets its own treatment once you have wrangling and programming in hand — but the idea is worth meeting here.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

EDA is a loop: question → visualize/transform/model → better questions
Variation within a variable: typical values, clusters, unusual values
Outliers are sometimes errors, sometimes discoveries. Investigate before deciding; disclose what you removed
Covariation between variables: pick the technique by variable type
Overplotting has several fixes: alpha, 2-D binning, binning one axis
Models let you strip out a dominant relationship to see what remains
